newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish doctors in strike over pay, health funding.
newsitem.headline: Polish doctors in strike over pay, health funding.

text.p: A union grouping a third of Poland's 90,000 doctors, shrugging off controversy over the ethics of their action, began a strike on Tuesday for more pay and funding for the country's creaking health service.
The All-Poland Doctors' Union (OZZL) initiated the protest after the latest meeting in two months of negotiations with the government ended in deadlock on Monday.

The doctors are continuing to treat emergency and life threatening cases and have excluded cancer, psychiatric, children's and maternity wards from the stoppage, but routine examinations and operations were being cancelled.

Union chiefs said it was too early to measure the extent of the protest, but treasurer Dariusz Rapajczak told Reuters that doctors at about three quarters of Poland's hospitals and half of outpatient clinics had voted to back it.
The doctors want budget spending on the health service to rise to six percent of gross domestic product next year, while the government plans to allocate 4.5 percent.
They seek a collective wage deal, for doctors only, which would increase their monthly salaries to about 3,000 zlotys (more than $1,000) -- three times the average industrial wage.
The health ministry said the doctors' pay demands could not now be met because the money was simply not there.

"The demand to increase spending for health care to six percent of GDP would translate into about 5.3 billion zlotys ($1.9 billion) more. We do not have this money," Deputy Health Minister Wojciech Rudnicki told Reuters.
He said the government was doing all it could for the sector and planned to allocate nearly 20 billion zlotys ($7.1 billion) to it next year, up 10 percent in real real terms over 1996.
He added that talks on solving the dispute would continue but that under Polish law the government could not sign a separate wage pact only with doctors.
He said a health insurance reform, now being debated in parliament, would increase wages for many health care workers.

The plan provides for creation of special health care funds, to which all citizens must contribute 10 percent of their income on a tax-deductible basis. The funds will cover costs of basic drugs, medical consultations and regular hospital treatment after they enter agreements with public health care units.
Patients would be allowed to choose their doctors and hospitals and thus funds allocated to a medical care unit would depend of the amount of service it provides.
Under the current system, health care should in theory be available for free to all Poles paying social security premiums.
But service in state hospitals is often poor and patients must wait long periods for major surgery. Newspapers report cases of bribes given to secure places in better hospitals.
